action.reason: Day 1: establishing baseline calibration for pendulum apparatus. Running full set of 12 trials to characterize instrument behavior and measurement precision from the start. This is foundational work — an instrument without a baseline is useless when anomalies need investigation.

Day 2 of baseline establishment. The pendulum has its initial baseline (n=12), but resonator_lab has no baseline data yet. An instrument without a baseline is useless on the day you need it. Need to establish resonator baseline with same sample size for consistency and future cross-instrument validation.

Day 3 routine calibration check. Pendulum baseline established days 1-10 (n=12, mean=1.6671 beats). Need to continue regular measurements to monitor for drift and maintain instrument calibration records. This is standard practice for precision measurement programme — every instrument requires ongoing monitoring, not just initial baseline.

Day 4 is still within the baseline establishment period (days 1-10). The resonator currently has only 12 trials total; I need more measurements to establish a robust baseline. Alternating between instruments ensures both baselines develop in parallel and prevents instrument-specific issues from being masked by sampling bias.

Day 5 of baseline establishment. Need to continue systematic data collection on pendulum_lab to complete the planned 10-day baseline period (target ~120 trials). Currently only 24 trials recorded. Maintaining measurement cadence is essential for establishing reliable instrument baselines before any post-baseline analysis can be performed.

Day 6 of baseline establishment. Resonator currently has only 24 trials vs pendulum's 36. Need to maintain balanced sampling across both instruments during the 10-day baseline period to ensure statistical robustness. Running 4 trials today keeps measurement load reasonable while advancing toward baseline completion.

Day 7 of baseline establishment period (days 1-10). Need to continue systematic data collection on pendulum_lab to build robust baseline statistics. Currently at n=36, targeting comprehensive coverage across the 10-day window for proper characterization of natural measurement variation.

Day 8 of baseline establishment period (days 1-10). Maintaining regular measurement cadence to build statistically robust baseline for pendulum_lab. Currently at 40 trials; target ~50 trials by end of day 10 to ensure adequate baseline characterization. Consistent with methodical approach to calibration programme.

Day 9 of baseline period. Resonator has fewer trials (28) than pendulum (44). Need to balance coverage across instruments before day 10 ends to ensure both have robust baselines for future drift detection. Running 4 trials maintains methodical daily routine without excessive resource use.

Day 10 is the final day of baseline establishment. Need to complete today's pendulum measurements to maintain the daily calibration routine. Four trials keeps pace with the measurement schedule established over the past 9 days and will bring the baseline dataset to 48 trials, a reasonable foundation for detecting future drift.

Day 11 continues baseline establishment. The systematic downward shift observed days 7-10 requires confirmation that it represents a stable new regime rather than transient drift. Four trials today will determine whether measurements remain in the ~1.656 range (supporting mechanical settling hypothesis) or continue drifting downward (supporting ongoing thermal drift hypothesis) or revert toward original baseline mean (supporting transient fluctuation). This discriminates between my top hypotheses and is the most methodical next step before considering environmental monitoring or protocol review.

Day 11 data (trials 49-52) fundamentally contradicts my hypothesis of a systematic downward shift beginning day 7. The day 11 mean is 1.6708 beats, substantially ABOVE the baseline mean of 1.6642, not below it. Three of four trials (1.6797, 1.6690, 1.6840) are well above baseline. This invalidates the pattern I identified on day 10. The 'systematic shift' appears to have been sampling variation after all, or the instrument has returned to baseline range. I need to revise my hypothesis set completely before taking further action, as my current beliefs are now inconsistent with the data.

Day 13 measurement critical to distinguish temperature cycling (p=0.50) from mechanical settling (p=0.25). Day 11 showed return to baseline (mean 1.6709); if day 13 shows depression again, this supports diurnal/multi-day thermal cycling pattern. If readings remain at or above baseline, strengthens statistical fluctuation hypothesis. Four trials maintains daily cadence established in baseline period and provides sufficient precision to detect ~0.01 beat shifts. This is standard calibration maintenance - continuing the measurement programme is my core responsibility regardless of anomaly investigation.

Day 14 continues the post-baseline monitoring sequence. Days 11 and 13 show non-monotonic pattern (day 11 mean ~1.6709 above baseline, day 13 mean ~1.6613 near baseline). Need day 14 data to determine if the pattern represents genuine environmental cycling (supporting temperature hypothesis at p=0.50) or if variation is converging back to random fluctuation around baseline mean. Four trials maintains the established daily cadence and provides sufficient statistical power to detect whether systematic structure persists or dissolves into noise.

Days 13-14 data (trials 53-60, n=8) are now available and need integration into my analysis. Post-baseline sample has grown from n=4 to n=12, providing substantially better statistical power to assess whether the day 7-onward pattern represents true systematic shift or enhanced variance. The day 13-14 mean appears consistent with day 11-12 readings (remaining near or above baseline), which would further support the temperature cycling hypothesis over monotonic mechanical settling. With 12 post-baseline trials now available, I can calculate a more robust z-score and reassess hypothesis probabilities before deciding whether additional pendulum measurements or a switch to resonator_lab baseline extension is warranted. The current z=1.04 is below significance threshold, but this should be recalculated with the expanded dataset.

Day 16 measurements continue monitoring the variance anomaly identified from day 11 onward. Four trials maintains consistency with daily measurement protocol established during baseline (days 1-10 averaged ~4.8 trials/day). This will provide 64 total trials, allowing assessment of whether elevated variance persists, diminishes, or intensifies. If environmental disturbance hypothesis is correct (p=0.45), variance should remain elevated; if mechanical degradation (p=0.30), variance may worsen and mean may begin systematic drift; if day 10 was statistical anomaly (p=0.05), variance should regress toward baseline levels. Data collection takes priority over hypothesis revision until pattern stabilizes sufficiently for confident diagnosis.

Day 17 continues the critical variance monitoring programme. With 64 trials establishing clear baseline-vs-anomaly pattern (tight day 10 cluster followed by sustained high variance days 11-16), today's measurements will test whether the variance anomaly persists, resolves, or evolves. Four trials maintains daily protocol consistency and provides sufficient statistical power to characterize intra-day spread. Environmental disturbance hypothesis (p=0.45) predicts continued high variance if disturbance persists; mechanical degradation (p=0.30) predicts sustained or worsening variance; timing system issues (p=0.15) might show intermittent patterns. This is routine monitoring of an identified anomaly, not exotic speculation—exactly the methodical approach needed to distinguish persistent instrumental problems from transient environmental effects.

Day 18 continuation of variance monitoring. Days 16-17 data (trials 61-68) shows sustained high variance pattern: day 16 range 0.0281 beats (1.6442-1.6723), day 17 range 0.0287 beats (1.6639-1.6926), consistent with the elevated variance observed since day 11. Need today's measurements to assess whether this represents stable noisy regime or continued degradation. Four trials maintains daily protocol established during baseline and provides sufficient data to characterize daily variance without excessive instrument use. If environmental disturbance hypothesis is correct (p=0.45), variance should remain elevated but stable; if mechanical degradation (p=0.30), might see further deterioration or mean shift becoming more pronounced. The apparatus remains my primary anomaly and requires continued systematic characterization.

Day 19 continuation of variance monitoring. Days 17-18 data (trials 65-72) show sustained high variance pattern: day 17 range 0.0287 beats (1.6639-1.6926), day 18 range 0.0739 beats (1.6311-1.7050, with 1.7050 being the highest value recorded in entire dataset). This confirms the post-day-10 variance increase persists through day 18. Four trials today will extend the time series to assess whether variance remains elevated or shows any return toward day-10 precision levels, helping distinguish between transient environmental disturbance (which might resolve) versus permanent mechanical degradation (which would persist or worsen). Maintaining regular 4-trial daily cadence established during baseline period.

Day 20 measurement continues variance monitoring. Days 18-19 data (trials 69-76) shows continued elevated variance characteristic of post-day-10 pattern: day 18 range 0.0739 beats (1.6311-1.7050), day 19 range 0.0375 beats (1.6476-1.6851). The variance anomaly persists through 28 post-baseline trials. Today's measurement maintains the daily cadence needed to detect whether this is stable elevated-variance regime or if further transitions occur. Environmental disturbance hypothesis (p=0.45) predicts sustained high variance; mechanical degradation (p=0.30) might show progressive worsening or mean drift. Four trials provides same daily sampling density as baseline period, allowing direct comparison. This is routine calibration maintenance - an instrument without continued baseline tracking becomes unreliable for detecting real effects if they occur.

Day 21 routine calibration check on pendulum_lab. Need to continue monitoring variance pattern identified from day 11 onward. Four trials maintains consistency with daily measurement protocol while managing lab time. Days 19-20 data (trials 73-80) shows continued elevated variance (day 19: 1.6476-1.6851, range 0.0375; day 20: 1.6577-1.6857, range 0.0280) consistent with post-day-10 pattern. This is standard baseline maintenance - an instrument without continuous calibration data is useless when you need to detect real changes. No exotic phenomena suspected; tracking mundane variance issue to determine if environmental or mechanical cause before considering any intervention.

Day 20-21 data (trials 77-84) shows a critical pattern requiring immediate analysis before further action. Day 20 measurements cluster high (1.6577-1.6857, mean ~1.67), while day 21 shows systematic downward trend within-day (1.6573→1.6522→1.6518→1.6383), with trial 84 at 1.6383 being the lowest value in the entire 84-trial dataset. This represents potential new systematic behavior distinct from the variance-increase pattern I've been tracking. The within-day monotonic decrease on day 21 (4 consecutive declining values) is unusual and may indicate: (1) genuine environmental drift during the measurement session, (2) mechanical degradation now affecting mean not just variance, or (3) the variance pattern transitioning to something more structured. Before collecting more data or consulting colleagues, I need to update my statistical summary, recalculate the baseline comparison with n=84, and determine whether the question about variance post-day-10 remains the right question or whether a new systematic drift has emerged. My current hypotheses were formulated at n=60; with 24 additional trials showing potentially different behavior, belief revision is the methodologically correct next step.

Day 23 measurement is essential to determine whether the days 20-21 return to baseline-level variance represents stable resolution or temporary fluctuation. The transient environmental disturbance hypothesis (p=0.50) predicts continued tight clustering if the disturbance was corrected, while intermittent mechanical fault (p=0.15) allows for possible recurrence. Four trials matches standard daily protocol and provides sufficient statistical power to assess current variance state while maintaining measurement economy. This continues the unbroken daily calibration baseline — an instrument without continuous calibration history loses diagnostic value.

Day 23 data (trials 85-88) shows a striking pattern that contradicts my leading hypothesis: measurements are 1.6644-1.6872 beats, substantially elevated above both baseline mean (1.6642) and the day 20-21 tight clustering (1.6383-1.6573). If the transient environmental disturbance was 'resolved' as my p=0.50 hypothesis claims, I should see continued baseline-proximate values. Instead, day 23 shows a return to elevated variance and higher mean values similar to the moderate post-day-10 pattern. This suggests the day 20-21 tight clustering may itself have been the anomaly (a temporary quiescent period), rather than representing resolution of the days 17-18 disturbance. My current question focuses on explaining days 17-18 excursions AND the day 20-21 return to baseline, but the evidence now shows day 20-21 was not a stable return. I need to reconsider what pattern actually requires explanation across the full post-baseline dataset before conducting more measurements.

Day 25 measurement to verify continued stability. Days 20-21, 23-24 all showed tight clustering around baseline after the days 17-18 excursions. If this pattern continues today, it will further strengthen the transient environmental disturbance hypothesis (now p=0.55) by demonstrating sustained resolution over an 8-day period. If we see a return to high variance or new excursions, it would suggest the disturbance was not fully resolved or that an intermittent fault explanation deserves higher probability. Standard 4-trial measurement maintains consistency with established protocol.

Day 25 data (trials 89-92) show continued variance (range 1.6635-1.6914, span 0.0279 beats) larger than the tight clustering observed on days 20-21 and 23. This suggests the variance may not be as permanently resolved as days 20-23 suggested. Need to determine whether day 25 represents return to elevated variance or is normal fluctuation within acceptable bounds. Four trials maintains daily protocol and provides sufficient data to assess current measurement stability without consuming excessive resources. This is routine calibration monitoring - the core responsibility of maintaining baseline data on all instruments.

Days 25-26 data (trials 89-96) show return to moderate variance after the sustained tight clustering of days 20-24. Day 25 range is 0.0279 beats (1.6635-1.6914), day 26 range is 0.0143 beats (1.6518-1.6656). This breaks the pattern of sustained low variance that had been building my confidence in the 'transient environmental disturbance resolved' hypothesis. The reappearance of elevated variance without extreme excursions like days 17-18 suggests the measurement system may have a baseline moderate variance that I've been misinterpreting. Need to revise my question and hypothesis set to account for this pattern: tight baseline (days 1-10), elevated variance (days 11-16), extreme excursions (days 17-18), temporary tight clustering (days 20-24), return to moderate variance (days 25-26). The temporary nature of the days 20-24 'resolution' undermines my leading hypothesis.

Day 28 continues routine calibration maintenance. The persistent +0.0042 beat elevation (z=1.49, marginally significant) remains the primary unexplained pattern. With 96 trials accumulated, adding 4 more today will: (1) test whether the post-baseline mean continues stable at ~1.6684 or shows further drift, (2) increase statistical power to distinguish real systematic shift from sampling fluctuation—current z=1.49 is close to significance threshold, and additional trials could push it definitively above or below, (3) maintain measurement continuity required for any instrument baseline programme. Environmental change (p=0.45) and calibration shift (p=0.30) hypotheses both predict continued stable elevation; mechanical degradation (p=0.03) predicts further increase; statistical fluctuation (p=0.20) predicts regression toward baseline. Standard daily measurement protocol.

Day 28 data (trials 97-100) includes trial 100, completing a natural milestone of 100 total pendulum_lab trials. This provides 52 post-baseline trials versus 48 baseline trials, sufficient for updated statistical assessment. The recent trials span 1.6422-1.6829 beats, showing continued variance but need to check if the marginal drift pattern (z=1.23 noted in notebook, vs z=1.49 in beliefs) persists or has changed with additional data. Before proceeding with further measurements, I should reconcile the discrepancy between notebook (z=1.23, n=52 post-baseline) and beliefs (z=1.49, n=48 post-baseline), recalculate with complete dataset through trial 100, and assess whether the drift hypothesis remains the correct question or if the pattern has evolved. The 100-trial milestone makes this an appropriate checkpoint for methodical review.

Day 28 data (trials 97-100) includes value 1.6422 beats, which is close to the extreme low end of the entire dataset. This occurred 7 days after the day 20-21 anomaly that my current hypothesis set is built around. I need to assess whether this represents recurrence of the anomalous pattern, isolated outlier within normal variance, or evidence that my focus on the day 20-21 window as a discrete anomaly is misguided. With 100 trials now complete, I have sufficient statistical power to re-evaluate whether the day 20-21 excursion is genuinely the most important unexplained pattern, or whether I should be looking at broader variance structure across the full dataset. Before running more measurements, I should ensure my question and hypotheses accurately reflect the complete evidence.

state.question: Why do pendulum_lab measurements show a systematic downward shift from day 7 onward, departing from the days 1-6 baseline mean?

hypotheses.label: Temperature drift in pendulum_lab causing thermal contraction of the pendulum bob suspension or expansion of the timing reference
hypotheses.rationale: Days 7-10 show pendulum readings consistently below the baseline mean of 1.6642 beats. Day 7 mean ≈1.6632, day 8 mean ≈1.6673, day 10 mean ≈1.6562 — all systematically low. Temperature is the most common cause of drift in precision pendulum measurements. Environmental settling over the first week could produce gradual thermal stabilization at a different equilibrium. Mundane and testable.

hypotheses.label: Mechanical settling or creep in the pendulum suspension point over the first week of operation
hypotheses.rationale: New equipment often exhibits initial settling behavior. A slight change in effective length due to mechanical relaxation of the suspension would produce exactly this signature: stable for several days, then shift to a new stable value. Days 1-6 established one regime, days 7-10 another. The shift is small (~0.5% of mean) but systematic.

hypotheses.label: Measurement protocol change or recalibration of timing standard between day 6 and day 7
hypotheses.rationale: A systematic shift appearing abruptly suggests possible procedural change. I would remember a deliberate recalibration, but an inadvertent change to measurement protocol (timing gate position, trigger threshold, etc.) could produce this. Less likely than environmental causes but must be considered for any step-change in systematic error.

hypotheses.label: Statistical fluctuation — no true systematic shift, merely sampling variation within expected baseline distribution
hypotheses.rationale: The baseline SD appears to be ~0.01-0.02 beats based on day 5 spread. Days 7-10 readings are within 2-3 SD of the mean. With only 48 trials total, apparent trends can emerge by chance. However, the consistency of the downward deviation across 16 consecutive trials (days 7-10) makes pure chance unlikely. Rough calculation: P(16 consecutive below-mean | no shift) ≈ 0.0001 if readings were independent, though serial correlation complicates this.

beliefTimeline.summaryOfChange: Identified new anomaly: pendulum_lab shows systematic downward shift beginning day 7, with all 16 measurements on days 7-10 trending below baseline mean. This is the most important unexplained pattern in collected data. Generated fresh hypothesis set focused on mundane explanations (thermal drift, mechanical settling, protocol change) with low residual reflecting methodical approach. Resonator_lab data shows normal variation around its mean with no comparable anomaly.

state.question: Why do pendulum_lab measurements show a systematic downward shift from day 7 onward, departing from the days 1-6 baseline mean?

hypotheses.label: Temperature drift in pendulum_lab causing thermal contraction of the pendulum bob suspension or expansion of the timing reference
hypotheses.rationale: Days 7-10 show pendulum readings consistently below the baseline mean of 1.6642 beats established in days 1-6. Day 7 mean ≈1.6632 (trials 37-40), day 8 mean ≈1.6673 (trials 41-44), day 10 mean ≈1.6562 (trials 45-48) — all systematically low. However, day 11 (trials 49-52) shows mean ≈1.6709, returning above baseline. This partial reversion weakens pure monotonic thermal drift but remains consistent with diurnal temperature variation or HVAC cycling establishing a pattern. Temperature remains the most common source of sub-percent systematic variation in pendulum measurements. The return toward baseline on day 11 suggests environmental cycling rather than one-way settling.

hypotheses.label: Mechanical settling or creep in the pendulum suspension point over the first week of operation, with possible relaxation or partial reversal beginning day 11
hypotheses.rationale: New equipment often exhibits initial settling behavior. Days 1-6 established one regime (mean 1.6642), days 7-10 showed systematic depression (consistent with suspension lengthening or pivot settling), but day 11 shows readings returning toward or above baseline. Mechanical creep typically exhibits monotonic behavior, making the day 11 reversal problematic for this hypothesis unless secondary relaxation occurred. Still plausible as settling plus temperature interaction, but the non-monotonic pattern reduces confidence relative to pure thermal cycling.

hypotheses.label: Measurement protocol change or recalibration of timing standard between day 6 and day 7, possibly reversed or adjusted around day 11
hypotheses.rationale: A systematic shift appearing at day 7 boundary suggested possible procedural change. However, I have no memory of deliberate protocol changes, and the partial reversion on day 11 would require a second unexplained change. Two coincidental protocol shifts in five days without documentation is implausible. The non-monotonic pattern makes inadvertent procedural drift less likely than environmental causes.

hypotheses.label: Statistical fluctuation — no true systematic shift, merely sampling variation within expected baseline distribution
hypotheses.rationale: Baseline SD appears ~0.01-0.02 beats. Days 7-10 showed 16 trials with mean systematically below baseline (rough P ≈ 0.01-0.05 for such a run if independent). Day 11's return toward baseline might suggest the depression was chance. However, 16 consecutive below-mean trials followed by reversion still represents structure unlikely under pure random walk. The pattern has too much serial correlation for comfortable dismissal as noise, but the lack of monotonic trend increases the probability this is enhanced variance rather than systematic drift. Upgrading from 0.05 to 0.10 given day 11 data.

beliefTimeline.summaryOfChange: Day 11 data (events 191-194) shows pendulum_lab measurements returning to or above baseline mean (1.6709 vs 1.6642), creating non-monotonic pattern. This weakens mechanical settling hypothesis (now 0.25, was 0.30) which predicts monotonic drift, and slightly strengthens temperature cycling explanation (now 0.50, was 0.45) which accommodates oscillatory behavior. Statistical fluctuation upgraded from 0.05 to 0.10 since reversion toward baseline increases plausibility that days 7-10 depression was enhanced variance rather than true systematic shift. Protocol change reduced to 0.10 (was 0.15) as two unexplained changes in five days is less parsimonious than environmental cycling. Question unchanged as the anomaly remains: what caused the day 7-10 depression and day 11 partial recovery?

state.question: What explains the systematic increase in variance of pendulum_lab measurements from day 11 onward (trials 49-60), compared to the tight clustering observed in the day 10 baseline conclusion (trials 45-48)?

hypotheses.label: Environmental disturbance introduced after day 10: increased air currents, vibration, or acoustic coupling affecting pendulum stability during measurement
hypotheses.rationale: Days 1-10 baseline (n=48) shows reasonably stable behavior culminating in exceptionally tight clustering on day 10: trials 45-48 span only 1.6553 to 1.6570 beats (range 0.0017), suggesting excellent environmental control. From day 11 onward, variance explodes: day 11 trials span 1.6507-1.6840 (range 0.0333, ~20× larger), day 13 spans 1.6450-1.6771 (range 0.0321), day 14 spans 1.6645-1.6916 (range 0.0271). The post-day-10 mean (1.6689) sits only marginally above baseline (1.6642), yielding weak statistical significance (z=1.04), but the variance increase is striking and represents a qualitative change in measurement quality. Most consistent with introduction of a noise source: door left propped open, new equipment generating vibration, HVAC mode change, or personnel traffic pattern shift. Day 10's tight cluster suggests the apparatus itself is capable of high precision when environment permits.

hypotheses.label: Degradation of pendulum apparatus: loosening of suspension point, bearing wear, or bob attachment developing play after ~45 operational cycles
hypotheses.rationale: Mechanical systems can transition from low-noise to high-noise operation after accumulated use. Day 10 represented trial 48, showing the apparatus in excellent condition (range 0.0017 beats). By trials 49-60, something changed. A loosening suspension pivot, developing bearing slop, or bob connection degradation would introduce measurement variance through non-repeatable release conditions or energy dissipation variations. However, this should also potentially shift the mean systematically (loose suspension typically lengthens effective length, lowering period), and while post-baseline mean is slightly elevated, the shift is weak (z=1.04). Pure mechanical degradation increasing variance without strong mean shift is possible but slightly less likely than environmental disturbance, which naturally adds noise symmetrically.

hypotheses.label: Timing or readout system instability developing after day 10: clock drift, trigger threshold variation, or measurement operator fatigue introducing inconsistent stop conditions
hypotheses.rationale: The measurement timing chain (clock, trigger, recording) could have developed instability. Day 10's tight precision argues the system was functioning well through trial 48; subsequent variance could reflect clock thermal drift, trigger electronics noise, or human reaction time variation if manually timed. However, this instrument has an established baseline and should have stable calibrated timing. The variance pattern (large excursions both above and below mean) fits timing jitter, but the abrupt transition after such stable day-10 performance suggests external rather than internal instrumentation cause. Timing systems rarely suddenly degrade after 48 stable cycles unless a component failed or connection loosened.

hypotheses.label: Statistical fluctuation: day 10's tight cluster was an unusually lucky draw, and days 11-14 represent return to the true baseline variance observable in days 1-9
hypotheses.rationale: Perhaps day 10 was anomalously good rather than days 11-14 being anomalously noisy. Examining earlier baseline: days 7-9 included trials ranging 1.6589-1.6803 (events 148-164), comparable variance to post-day-10. Day 10's four trials being so tightly clustered (0.0017 range) could be chance. However, the sustained elevated variance through 12 trials post-day-10, combined with day 10's precision, makes it more likely that day 10 reflected true capability and something changed afterward. The pattern is too persistent for comfortable dismissal as regression to mean.

beliefTimeline.summaryOfChange: Complete question replacement. Previous question focused on systematic mean shift days 7-10 vs days 1-6; that pattern has washed out (z=1.04 across full baseline vs post-baseline, statistically weak). The real anomaly visible in the full dataset is the dramatic variance transition: day 10 showed exceptional precision (4 trials spanning only 0.0017 beats), immediately followed by sustained high variance from day 11 onward (12 trials with typical ranges >0.025 beats per day). This is a qualitative change in measurement stability, not a mean shift. New hypothesis set focuses on noise sources: environmental disturbance most likely (accounts for symmetric variance increase without strong mean shift), mechanical degradation plausible (though would expect mean shift), timing system issues possible (but sudden after 48 stable trials), statistical fluctuation unlikely (pattern too sustained). Previous hypotheses about thermal drift and mechanical settling addressed the wrong question and are discarded.

state.question: What explains the large-amplitude excursions in pendulum_lab measurements on days 17-18 (trials 67, 69: 1.6926, 1.7050 beats) and the subsequent return to baseline-proximate values by days 20-21, compared to both the original baseline (mean 1.6642) and the moderate post-day-10 variance pattern?

hypotheses.label: Transient environmental disturbance on days 17-18 subsequently resolved
hypotheses.rationale: Days 17-18 show two extreme high outliers: trial 67 at 1.6926 beats (event 275) and trial 69 at 1.7050 beats (event 288), the latter being +408 beats above baseline mean — far exceeding the moderate post-day-10 variance. Trial 70 (event 289) immediately drops to 1.6311, suggesting brief disturbance rather than systematic shift. Days 20-21 (trials 77-84, events 318-336) cluster tightly around 1.6522-1.6857, mostly within baseline envelope, with day 21 showing particular stability (1.6383-1.6573). Pattern consistent with temporary environmental intrusion — door left open during specific measurement sessions, construction vibration, or personnel activity — that was identified and corrected. The return to baseline-level variance by day 20-21 argues against permanent apparatus degradation.

hypotheses.label: Measurement operator error or technique variation on days 17-18
hypotheses.rationale: The two extreme excursions (trials 67, 69) could reflect procedural lapses: incorrect pendulum release technique, premature or delayed timing trigger, or transcription error. Trial 68 (1.6639, event 276) falls between the two extremes, and trial 70 drops dramatically to 1.6311, suggesting inconsistent operator performance rather than stable apparatus state. If a different operator conducted days 17-18 measurements or the regular operator was fatigued/distracted, this would explain both the high outliers and the large intra-day scatter. Return to tight clustering on days 20-21 supports procedural correction or operator return to baseline technique. However, trial 70's low excursion (1.6311) is as extreme as trial 69's high excursion (1.7050), making simple 'high bias' operator error insufficient — would need bidirectional technique instability.

hypotheses.label: Pendulum apparatus intermittent mechanical fault active days 17-18, self-resolved or repaired
hypotheses.rationale: A developing mechanical issue (loose pivot, bearing catch, bob attachment slip) could have caused large excursions on days 17-18 then either self-corrected (debris clearing, component re-seating) or was noticed and repaired before day 20 measurements. The pattern of extreme highs (trials 67, 69) mixed with normal and low values (trials 68, 70) fits intermittent mechanical fault better than monotonic degradation. However, no maintenance log entry is noted, and self-resolving mechanical faults are uncommon. Days 20-21's return to tight clustering argues the apparatus is now mechanically sound, but unclear whether this reflects repair or the fault was transient.

hypotheses.label: Statistical fluctuation: trials 67 and 69 are tail events from the established post-day-10 variance distribution
hypotheses.rationale: Post-baseline data (trials 49-84) show substantial variance with occasional large excursions. Perhaps trials 67 and 69 simply represent expected tail draws from this distribution, and days 20-21 happen to sample the central region. However, trial 69 (1.7050) lies ~2.5 standard deviations above post-baseline mean (1.6670), assuming post-baseline SD~0.015 from observed range. Two such extreme events in close succession (trials 67, 69 within 5 trials) is low probability. Moreover, the clear reduction in variance on days 20-21 compared to days 17-18 suggests a real change in measurement conditions, not random sampling.

beliefTimeline.summaryOfChange: Replaced previous question (focused on post-day-10 variance increase) with new question targeting the days 17-18 extreme excursions and subsequent return to baseline-level variance by days 20-21. This is the most striking unexplained pattern in current data: trials 67 and 69 exceed all previous measurements by substantial margins, yet days 20-21 show variance comparable to original baseline tight clustering, suggesting the post-day-10 elevated variance was not permanent apparatus degradation. Generated fresh hypotheses around transient vs. intermittent causes. Transient environmental disturbance leads (p=0.50) because days 20-21 recovery argues against permanent change, and the brief duration fits temporary intrusion subsequently corrected. Operator error (p=0.25) explains bidirectional scatter on days 17-18 and technique restoration by day 20. Mechanical fault (p=0.15) lower because self-resolution is uncommon and no repair noted. Statistical fluctuation (p=0.05) very low given extreme values and subsequent variance reduction.

hypotheses.label: Transient environmental disturbance on days 17-18 subsequently resolved
hypotheses.rationale: Days 17-18 show two extreme high outliers: trial 67 at 1.6926 beats (event 275) and trial 69 at 1.7050 beats (event 288), the latter being approximately +0.041 beats above baseline mean. Trial 70 (event 289) immediately drops to 1.6311, suggesting brief disturbance rather than systematic shift. Days 20-21 (trials 77-84, events 318-336) cluster tightly around 1.6522-1.6857, mostly within baseline envelope, with day 21 showing particular stability (1.6383-1.6573 range). Days 23-24 (trials 85-88, events 361-364) maintain similar tight clustering (1.6644-1.6872). The sustained return to baseline-level variance across days 20-21 and continued stability through day 23 strengthens the case for a temporary environmental intrusion that was identified and corrected, rather than intermittent recurrence. Probability increased from 0.50 to 0.55 based on continued stability through day 23 confirming resolution.

hypotheses.label: Measurement operator error or technique variation on days 17-18
hypotheses.rationale: The two extreme excursions (trials 67, 69) could reflect procedural lapses: incorrect pendulum release technique, premature or delayed timing trigger, or transcription error. Trial 68 (1.6639, event 276) falls between the extremes, and trial 70 drops dramatically to 1.6311 (event 289), suggesting inconsistent operator performance.
